title: Mae Jemison: Doctor and Astronaut
summary: How Mae Jemison studied engineering and medicine, served as a doctor in Africa, and in 1992 became the first Black woman to travel to space.
poll: Anyone can reach a big dream if they work hard enough.

versions.title: Mae Jemison Goes to Space
versions.text:
As a girl, Mae Jemison had a dream. She wanted to go to space. At night, she would look up at the stars.

Mae grew up in a big city. It was in the United States. She loved to read. She loved science. She loved to dance, too. Back then, not a lot of girls like her did science. But Mae did not give up.

Mae went off to a big school at just 16. She learned to plan and make things. Then she learned to be a doctor. As a doctor, she went to Africa. She helped sick folks there for over two years.

Then Mae tried to join the space team. Lots of people tried. Just a few got in. Mae was one of them! Now she was an astronaut.

In 1992, Mae rode a space shuttle up to space. She was the first Black woman to go. She was there for eight days. She did tests. She learned how the body works in space.

Now Mae helps kids learn science. Her dream came true. She hopes yours will, too!

versions.title: Mae Jemison: Doctor and Astronaut
versions.text:
When Mae Jemison was a young girl, she had a big dream. She wanted to travel into space. At night, she looked at the stars and hoped to explore them one day.

Mae was born in 1956 and grew up in Chicago. She loved to read about space, science, and nature, and she also loved to dance. Watching astronauts on TV helped inspire her. In those days, very few women and very few Black people worked as scientists. Some people doubted that Mae could become one. But she did not give up.

Mae went to college when she was only 16. She studied chemical engineering, which is the science of finding ways to make useful things. Later, she went to medical school and became a doctor. Then she worked as a volunteer doctor in two African countries. She cared for people who were sick.

In 1987, Mae was chosen to join NASA, the American space agency. About two thousand people had tried, but only fifteen were picked.

In 1992, Mae flew into space on the space shuttle Endeavour. She became the first Black woman to travel to space. In about eight days, the shuttle went around Earth in orbit more than one hundred times. Mae did an experiment on how the human body changes in space.

Today, Mae helps young people learn about science. She shows them that a dream can come true through hard work.

versions.title: Mae Jemison: Doctor, Engineer, and Astronaut
versions.text:
When Mae Jemison was a young girl, she had an enormous dream. She wanted to travel into space, and at night she gazed at the stars and imagined exploring them someday.

Mae was born in Alabama in 1956 and grew up in Chicago, where she loved reading about astronomy, science, and nature, and where she also studied dance. Watching astronauts on television helped inspire her, and so did a science fiction program that featured a Black woman working aboard a spaceship. At that time, very few women and very few Black Americans worked as scientists, and some people doubted that Mae could become one. However, her determination never weakened.

Mae entered Stanford University when she was only 16 and earned a degree in chemical engineering, the science of designing processes to manufacture useful materials. Afterward, she attended medical school and became a doctor. She then served as a volunteer doctor in Sierra Leone and Liberia, two countries in West Africa.

In 1987, Mae was chosen to join NASA, the American space agency, after competing against approximately two thousand applicants for only fifteen places.

In 1992, she flew into space aboard the space shuttle Endeavour, becoming the first Black woman to travel to space and a true pioneer. During the nearly eight-day mission, the shuttle circled Earth more than one hundred times. Meanwhile, Mae worked on experiments investigating how weightlessness affects the human body, including bone cells and motion sickness.

In 1993, Mae left NASA and founded a technology company, as well as an international science camp for students. She even appeared in an episode of Star Trek, the same science fiction series that had inspired her as a child.

Mae's journey shows that a barrier can be broken through effort and courage. Today, she encourages young people, especially girls, to study science, and she reminds them that curiosity and hard work can make even the boldest dream come true.

Afterward, she attended medical school and became a physician, and she subsequently served as a volunteer doctor in Sierra Leone and Liberia, two countries in West Africa, where she was responsible for the health of numerous American volunteers.

More recently, she has led a project that encourages research into the technologies humans would need to travel to another star.

versions.title: Mae Jemison: Doctor, Engineer, and Astronaut
versions.text:
As a young girl gazing nightly at the stars scattered across the Chicago sky, Mae Jemison held a very big dream: to travel into space herself, a dream that seemed, in that era, almost out of reach for a Black girl growing up in America.

Born in Alabama in 1956, Jemison was raised mostly in Chicago, where she eagerly read books about astronomy, biology, and the natural sciences while also training seriously in dance. Her imagination was further sparked by television shows about astronauts and by a science fiction show with a Black woman serving aboard a spacecraft. At that time, very few women and an even smaller share of Black Americans worked in science, and skeptics often doubted whether Jemison could really reach such an unlikely goal; even so, her determination never wavered despite a good deal of social doubt.

Enrolling at Stanford University at just sixteen years of age, she earned a degree in chemical engineering, the field that designs processes for making useful materials. She later attended medical school, qualified as a physician, and then volunteered as a doctor in Sierra Leone and Liberia, two West African nations, where she took charge of protecting the health of many American volunteers working abroad.

In 1987, having competed against about two thousand other applicants for only fifteen open spots, Jemison was chosen to join NASA, America's national space agency, an achievement reflecting extraordinary competitive distinction.

By 1992, she had flown into space aboard the space shuttle Endeavour, becoming thereby the first Black woman ever to reach orbit and establishing herself as a true pioneer. Throughout this nearly eight-day mission, during which the shuttle circled Earth upwards of one hundred times, Jemison conducted careful experiments investigating how weightlessness affects the human body, examining phenomena such as bone cell loss and motion sickness. This cooperative mission with Japan included dozens of scientific experiments, ranging from materials research to studies of living organisms in orbit.

Resigning from NASA in 1993, Jemison later established both a technology company and an international science camp for students, even appearing in an episode of Star Trek, the very show that had once inspired her childhood dream. More recently, she has led an effort to study the technology humans will someday need for travel between the stars.

Jemison's remarkable path clearly shows that seemingly huge barriers can indeed be overcome through steady persistence and real courage. Today, she actively encourages young people, particularly girls, to pursue scientific careers, often stressing that curiosity combined with steady dedication can make even the boldest dream come true.

versions.title: Mae Jemison: Doctor, Engineer, and Astronaut
versions.text:
As a young girl gazing nightly toward the stars scattered across the Chicago sky, Mae Jemison harbored an extraordinarily audacious ambition: to journey personally into outer space, a dream that appeared, given the social realities of that era, almost implausibly unattainable for a Black girl coming of age in mid-twentieth-century America.

Born in Alabama in 1956, Jemison was raised predominantly within Chicago, where she voraciously consumed literature spanning astronomy, biology, and the broader natural sciences while concurrently pursuing rigorous training in dance. Her imagination was further ignited by televised broadcasts documenting astronauts' exploits and by a science fiction program portraying a Black woman serving competently aboard an interstellar spacecraft. During that particular historical period, remarkably few women and an even smaller proportion of Black Americans occupied recognized scientific professions, and persistent skeptics frequently doubted whether Jemison could realistically accomplish such an improbable ambition; nevertheless, her determination remained fundamentally unshaken despite pervasive societal discouragement and institutional obstacles.

Matriculating at Stanford University at merely sixteen years of age, she earned an undergraduate degree in chemical engineering, the specialized discipline concerned with designing complex industrial processes for manufacturing useful materials at scale. She subsequently completed medical school, qualified formally as a licensed physician, and thereafter volunteered as a doctor throughout Sierra Leone and Liberia, two West African nations, where she assumed substantial responsibility for safeguarding the medical welfare of numerous American volunteers stationed abroad under challenging conditions.

In 1987, having competed against approximately two thousand rival applicants for a mere fifteen available positions, Jemison was ultimately selected to join NASA, the United States' national space agency, a selection reflecting an extraordinary degree of competitive distinction and professional preparation.

By 1992, she had successfully journeyed into orbit aboard the space shuttle Endeavour, thereby becoming the first Black woman ever to reach space and firmly establishing herself as an authentic pioneer within the aerospace profession. Throughout this demanding, nearly eight-day mission, during which the shuttle circled Earth upwards of one hundred times, Jemison conducted sophisticated scientific experiments investigating precisely how weightlessness affects human physiology, examining phenomena including progressive bone cell deterioration and persistent motion sickness. This cooperative international mission, undertaken jointly alongside Japan, incorporated dozens of distinct scientific investigations ranging from materials research to detailed studies of living organisms under sustained orbital conditions.

Resigning from NASA in 1993, Jemison subsequently established both an independent technology enterprise and an international science camp designed for students, even appearing memorably in an episode of Star Trek, the identical science fiction series that had originally inspired her childhood aspirations decades earlier. More recently, she has directed an ambitious initiative encouraging rigorous research into the technologies humanity would eventually require to undertake genuine interstellar travel.

Jemison's remarkable professional trajectory powerfully demonstrates that seemingly insurmountable societal barriers can indeed be overcome through sustained, disciplined persistence and genuine courage in the face of considerable adversity. Today, she actively and visibly encourages young people, particularly girls from underrepresented backgrounds, to pursue demanding scientific careers, consistently emphasizing that intellectual curiosity combined with unwavering dedication can render even the most audacious, improbable dream genuinely achievable given sufficient time and resolve.

MID.modelAnswer: Mae Jemison was inspired by watching astronauts on television and by a science fiction show that featured a Black woman working on a spaceship. Her story could inspire a student today because even though some people doubted she could become a scientist, she studied chemical engineering, became a doctor, volunteered in two countries, and was chosen by NASA out of thousands of applicants. This shows a student that with hard work, a dream can really come true.

keyWords.definition: the feeling of having no weight, as astronauts float in space
keyWords.example: In weightlessness, a drop of water floats like a tiny ball.

keyWords.definition: a strong decision to keep trying even when things are hard
keyWords.example: With determination, he practiced until he could finish the race.

keyWords.definition: one of the first people to do something new
keyWords.example: She was a pioneer in using computers to study weather.

keyWords.definition: something that blocks the way or makes it hard to move forward
keyWords.example: Not speaking the language was a barrier at first, but she learned quickly.

keyWords.definition: an important trip or job with a special purpose
keyWords.example: The rescue mission brought all the hikers home safely.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea?
options: Mae Jemison became famous mainly as an actor.
Her determination carried her past barriers into space.
NASA missions are mainly about traveling to other stars.
Science fiction shows are more important than real science.
questions.why: The article shows how Mae overcame doubts and barriers through study and persistence to make history in space.

wrong.A: Her Star Trek appearance is a minor detail.
wrong.C: Her mission studied the human body while orbiting Earth.
wrong.D: The article does not compare the importance of fiction and science.

questions.stem: What did Mae study during the Endeavour mission?
options: How to grow food on the Moon
How to land a shuttle
How stars form
How weightlessness affects the human body
questions.why: The article says she conducted experiments on how weightlessness affects the body, including bone cells and motion sickness.

wrong.B: Landing is not described as her experiment.

questions.stem: Why is Mae's appearance on Star Trek meaningful?
options: She had always wanted to be an actor instead of a scientist.
It was in the series that had inspired her as a child.
It was her first job after college.
It helped her get chosen by NASA.
questions.why: The article notes the series had inspired her as a child, so appearing in it completed a circle in her story.

wrong.A: The article shows her goal was science and space.
wrong.C: It happened in 1993, long after college.
wrong.D: She was chosen by NASA in 1987, before the appearance.

questions.stem: In the article, the word barrier most nearly means —
options: an obstacle
a reward
a spacecraft
a type of school
questions.why: The article says a barrier can be overcome through persistence, so it is something that blocks the way.

wrong.B: A reward is something you receive, not something you overcome.
wrong.C: A spacecraft is the shuttle, not a barrier.
wrong.D: A barrier is not a school.

questions.stem: Which event happened FIRST?
options: Mae left NASA and founded a company.
Mae was selected by NASA.
Mae served as a volunteer doctor in West Africa.
Mae flew aboard Endeavour.
questions.why: Mae served in Sierra Leone and Liberia before being selected by NASA in 1987, flying in 1992, and leaving in 1993.

wrong.A: This happened in 1993, after her flight.
wrong.B: This happened in 1987, after her service in Africa.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe how few women and Black Americans worked as scientists at that time?
options: To explain why science is too difficult
To show the barriers Mae had to overcome
To argue that Mae should have chosen dance
To describe the strict rules NASA uses to choose astronauts
questions.why: This detail shows the obstacles Mae faced, making her achievement as a pioneer more meaningful.

wrong.A: The article does not say science is too difficult.
wrong.C: The article celebrates her science career.

questions.stem: How did Mae's medical training connect to her work in space?
options: She designed the shuttle's engines.
She treated sick people on the Moon.
She studied how weightlessness affects the human body.
It had no connection to her space work.
questions.why: As a physician, Mae was well prepared to conduct experiments on bone cells and motion sickness in space.

wrong.A: The article does not say she designed engines.
wrong.B: The mission orbited Earth; it did not go to the Moon.
wrong.D: Her experiments about the body connect directly to medicine.

questions.stem: What is the most likely reason Mae started a science camp and encourages girls to study science?
options: She wants others to overcome barriers as she did.
She wants to stop working in science.
She believes only astronauts should study science.
She wants to become a teacher of dance.
questions.why: Mae faced doubts herself, so helping young people, especially girls, study science helps them overcome similar barriers.

wrong.B: Starting a camp keeps her involved in science.
wrong.C: She encourages all young people, not just astronauts.
wrong.D: The camp is about science, not dance.

HIGH.prompt: Mae Jemison is called a pioneer. Explain what makes someone a pioneer and why Mae fits that description, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained what a pioneer is.
I gave at least two pieces of evidence about Mae.
I explained how the evidence shows she is a pioneer.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A pioneer is someone who overcomes barriers to do something that few or no people like them had done before. Mae Jemison fits this description because she became the first Black woman to travel to space, flying aboard the space shuttle Endeavour in 1992 despite living in a time when very few women or Black people worked as scientists. Her determination carried her from studying chemical engineering and medicine to being chosen by NASA out of about two thousand applicants, and once in orbit she conducted an experiment about weightlessness and the human body. This evidence shows that her mission broke barriers for the scientists who came after her.
